clue.text: New hope round university brought back atmosphere of elation

indicators.note: the reworked letters go round, enclosing, the abbreviation for university
new here means made afresh, so the letters of hope are put into a fresh order
brought back says the word for atmosphere is turned round and read right to left

parts.note: an atmosphere is an air, as in 'an air of mystery'

explanation.surface: A fresh hope on campus lifts the whole mood to one of elation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New' rearranges HOPE to EPHO, and 'round' wraps it about U to give EUPHO; 'brought back' turns AIR into RIA.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym: both name an intense feeling of happiness and excitement.

clue.text: Count us out after Unionist becomes oily

indicators.note: the anagram comes after the letter for Unionist, so that letter leads

parts.note: U is the abbreviation for Unionist in British politics

indicators.note: out here means disordered or not in place, so the letters of count us are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone counting votes leaves out a slippery Unionist politician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges COUNTUS to NCTUOUS, and 'after' puts it behind U.
explanation.definitionFit: Unctuous literally means greasy, and figuratively describes a smarmy manner, the same double sense oily has.

clue.text: Initially high, very high," cost of doomsday weapon

indicators.note: initially takes just the opening letter of the word high

parts.note: something that costs a bomb is very expensive, so a very high cost is a bomb in British slang

explanation.surface: A doomsday weapon begins with a price that is sky-high.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang a thing that 'costs a bomb' is very expensive, so a very high cost is a BOMB; the stray quote mark in the printed clue marks 'very high' as a phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: A hydrogen bomb is the thermonuclear weapon feared as able to end civilisation.

clue.text: Killer hurts they say; that could account for it

definitions.text: Killer hurts they say; that could account for it

parts.words: Killer hurts they say; that could account for it
parts.note: spoken aloud, killer hurts is kilohertz, a unit of how often a wave repeats; the clue asks what kind of measurement such units describe

explanation.surface: Someone is told a murderer is in pain and wonders what could explain it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Killer hurts' said aloud is 'kilohertz', the unit used for broadcast wavebands, so the thing that kilohertz accounts for is a band of the radio spectrum.
explanation.definitionFit: Kilohertz is the unit in which wireless broadcast bands are measured, so a kilohertz figure describes a band of the radio spectrum.

clue.text: Moving pictures by artist to be put up? It's elementary

indicators.note: in a down clue put up means raised, read from bottom to top, so the whole string is turned round

parts.note: cines is an old word for films, or moving pictures
RA is a Royal Academician, the usual crossword artist

explanation.surface: Films and a painter are hoisted up, with a hint at Sherlock Holmes's famous phrase.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be put up' turns CINESRA into the answer; 'It's elementary' means it is a chemical element, not Holmes's 'elementary'.
explanation.definitionFit: Arsenic is a chemical element, number 33 on the periodic table.

clue.text: Show sorrow for heartless devoutness

indicators.note: heartless removes the central letter, the heart, of the word for devoutness

parts.note: piety is religious devoutness

explanation.surface: Someone grieves for a faith that has lost its warmth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heartless' takes the middle E out of PIETY.
explanation.definitionFit: To feel compassion for someone is to grieve on their behalf, a synonym of showing sorrow for them.

clue.text: Criticise soundly a cashier's cigar

parts.note: to pan a show is to criticise it harshly

indicators.note: soundly, read as by sound, says the words are spelt as they are heard

parts.note: a bank teller is a cashier, and the 's stands for is, a link

explanation.surface: A thorough telling-off for a bank clerk over a cigar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'soundly' looks like 'thoroughly' but signals a homophone: 'pan a teller' said aloud gives the cigar's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A panatella is a long thin type of cigar.

clue.text: But elm, diseased, has to come down

indicators.note: diseased means unhealthy, out of order, so the letters of but elm are mixed up

explanation.surface: A sick elm tree has to be felled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'diseased' rearranges BUTELM; Dutch elm disease makes the surface plausible.
explanation.definitionFit: To tumble is to fall, which is coming down.

clue.text: Not told because one's lost?

parts.note: told in its old sense means counted, as with a bank teller, so the clue describes someone missing from a count because they have gone astray

explanation.surface: Someone left out of the story because they have gone missing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Told' means counted (as in telling votes or rosary beads), so a missing person who is not counted fits the whole phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: When a person is missing their whereabouts are unknown, so they are left out of the tally.

clue.text: Agreement to produce mains flex

parts.note: mains electricity is alternating current, AC
a flex is an electric cord or cable in British English

explanation.surface: A deal that delivers a power lead for the electricity supply.
explanation.walkthrough: In British English a 'flex' is an electric lead, and mains supply is AC.
explanation.definitionFit: An accord is a formal settlement between parties, a synonym of agreement.

clue.text: My son travelling round US city has to find another name

indicators.note: the reworked letters go round the abbreviation for the city
travelling means moving about, so the letters of my son are moved around

parts.note: NY is New York

explanation.surface: A boy travels round New York and needs a different name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'travelling' rearranges MYSON to SYNOM, and 'round' splits it to hold NY.
explanation.definitionFit: A word that means the same as another is an alternative name for the thing.

clue.text: British have followed teachers like Hazel

indicators.note: followed says the British pieces come after the teachers' union

parts.note: NUT is the National Union of Teachers
to own is to have or possess

explanation.surface: British staff take after their teachers, much as a girl named Hazel might.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hazel' is capitalised to look like a name, but it is the nut and its colour; the NUT is the National Union of Teachers, a UK trade union.
explanation.definitionFit: Nut-brown is the warm mid-brown colour of a ripe hazelnut.

clue.text: Feline let loose could kill these

definitions.text: Feline let loose could kill these

parts.note: a feline is a cat

indicators.note: loose means set free and in disorder, so the letters of let are rearranged

explanation.surface: A big cat on the loose is a threat to livestock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'loose' rearranges LET to TLE after CAT; the whole clue also describes what a big cat at large might kill.
explanation.definitionFit: Farm livestock such as cows are the prey an escaped big cat might attack.

clue.text: Extra classes for those not very good at adding?

definitions.text: Extra classes for those not very good at adding?

parts.words: Extra classes for those not very good at adding?
parts.note: a summer is someone who sums, so the clue pictures a school for poor adders, while the real sense is holiday-time courses

explanation.surface: Remedial lessons for weak arithmeticians.
explanation.walkthrough: Read a summer as a person who adds up: weak adders might need extra schooling.
explanation.definitionFit: Courses held in the long vacation are extra tuition outside the normal term.

clue.text: Most stingy about street poverty criterion

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the word for most stingy goes round the street abbreviation

parts.note: the meanest person is the most stingy

explanation.surface: The tightest people in the road set the test for hardship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' places ST inside MEANEST, after MEAN.
explanation.definitionFit: A test of income and savings decides whether someone is poor enough to qualify for state help.

clue.text: Almost where William came from to go to Jerusalem one time

indicators.note: to go to says the second piece is attached after the first
almost means not quite all, so the last letter of the place is dropped

parts.note: the philosopher William of Occam took his name from the village of Ockham, also spelt Occam
Sion is a variant spelling of Zion, a name for Jerusalem

explanation.surface: Someone from William's home town travels on to the holy city on a single trip.
explanation.walkthrough: William is the philosopher of Occam's razor; 'Almost' drops the final M. Sion is the older spelling of Zion.
explanation.definitionFit: An occasion is a particular instance when something happens, one time among others.

clue.text: Current cute expert has grasped name of slight friend

parts.note: AC is alternating current
quaint means attractively old-fashioned, cute

indicators.note: has grasped means holds within, so the expert word encloses the letter for name

parts.note: an ace is an expert

explanation.surface: A charming specialist knows the name of a casual friend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has grasped' places N inside ACE to give ANCE after AC and QUAINT.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone you know only a little is a casual contact rather than a close friend.

clue.text: Awful slob in prayer to forgive

indicators.note: in places the rearranged letters inside the prayer word

parts.note: an Ave, Ave Maria, is a prayer

indicators.note: awful means terrible, out of shape, so the letters of slob are mixed up

explanation.surface: A dreadful lazybones prays for pardon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Awful' turns SLOB into BSOL, and 'in' puts it within AVE.
explanation.definitionFit: To absolve is to free from guilt or sin, as a priest grants pardon.

clue.text: Depicting one as conservative in Foreign Office is a disaster

indicators.note: in puts the three pieces inside the abbreviation for the ministry

parts.note: FO is the Foreign Office, the British government foreign ministry
the Roman numeral I is one

explanation.surface: Portraying a Tory as being in the Foreign Office is a calamity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' places I, AS and C inside FO, the Foreign Office (Britain's foreign ministry); 'Depicting' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A fiasco is a humiliating failure, a complete flop.

clue.text: Material with which it's

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held, 'Material with which it's (6)', is cut short: TIS can come from it's, but no word for SUE remains, and a quoted search found no fuller text.

clue.text: Ghostly aspect to left and right, shimmering

indicators.note: shimmering means wavering and flickering, so the letters are shaken into a new order

explanation.surface: A ghost seems to waver on either side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shimmering' rearranges ASPECT plus L and R.
explanation.definitionFit: Spectral describes something like a phantom or apparition, so it means ghostly.

clue.text: High time to reverse positions of leg

indicators.note: to reverse positions says the two pieces swap places, so the time letter jumps to the front

parts.note: taken as the word itself

explanation.surface: It is high time somebody's leg changed position.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to reverse positions of' swaps HIGH and T, putting T in front.
explanation.definitionFit: The thigh is the upper part of the leg, so the part stands for the whole limb, a fairly loose definition.

clue.text: Pattern specially made for clients

indicators.note: specially made means reworked to order, so the letters of clients are rearranged

explanation.surface: A design tailored for customers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'specially made for' rearranges CLIENTS.
explanation.definitionFit: A stencil is a cut-out template used to reproduce a design.

clue.text: Cold fellow's stiff

parts.note: rigid means stiff, unbending

explanation.surface: A chilly man has gone rigid.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is a link word ('is').
explanation.definitionFit: Frigid means very cold, as in frigid air.

clue.text: Two out of four could be radical

definitions.text: Two out of four could be radical

parts.words: Two out of four could be radical
parts.note: two is what you get from four by taking its square, and the radical sign is the symbol used for that operation

explanation.surface: Half the members of a quartet turn out to be revolutionaries.
explanation.walkthrough: In maths two is the square base number that multiplies by itself to give four, and the √ symbol is called the radical; 'radical' looks political but is mathematical.
explanation.definitionFit: The square root of four is two, and in algebra a radical expression is one using the √ sign.

clue.text: Reap changes to sharpen sound in this?

indicators.note: changes means alters, so the letters of reap are rearranged

parts.note: to hone a blade is to sharpen it

explanation.surface: Gathering the harvest makes noises sharper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changes' rearranges REAP to EARP, then HONE follows.
explanation.definitionFit: A headphone piece held to the ear is where you hear audio.
